ai.summary: Slice is a React UI SDK and browser runtime library that combines a design system, component library, and abstractions over complex browser and realtime APIs into one composable package.
ai.tagline: A single package for theme, UI, browser APIs, and realtime product building.
emphasize: Composability across UI, stores, hooks, and browser APIs
Single-package design system and runtime model
Granular export strategy and build engineering
Real-world authoring and maintenance work, not just component demos
avoid: Describing it as only a component library
Reducing the project to visuals without mentioning architecture
Overstating maturity beyond the current pre-1.0 state
suggestedQuestions: What problem does Slice solve better than combining multiple libraries?
How does the export map and build system work?
What makes the theming model different?
How does Slice handle browser APIs and WebRTC?
limitations: Do not imply production scale beyond what is explicitly documented
Do not invent components or API features not present in the project content

header.title: React UI SDK
header.subtitle: Design language, component library, and browser API layer — all in one npm package. "Because piecing together multiple libraries to ship one feature stopped making sense."

items.title: Realtime right out-of-the box
items.description: Production-ready abstractions over WebRTC, WebSocket, and SSE — video, audio, screen sharing, and live data streams without the boilerplate.

items.title: Complete design system
items.description: A design language built into a single React provider. Fully customizable token system across colors, spacing, motion, typography, icons, and more.

items.title: Everything composes
items.description: Types flow between layers so the pieces fit together. Hooks return types the components already expect — less wiring, less glue code, more product.

items.title: Built to be lean
items.description: 98 granular export paths mean your bundle only includes what you actually use. Import from the root or go granular — tree-shaking handles the rest.

items.title: SSR ready, zero config
items.description: Full SSR and static rendering support for Next.js and Remix, out of the box. No wrappers, no workarounds — it just works.

blocks.text: Most frontend projects need the same things: a design system, a component library, and abstractions over complex APIs like WebRTC, etc. The typical answer - use multiple packages, none of which "speak" each other.
Result? Wasted time (often days) wiring them together, wrangling types, writing glue code — before actually producing product logic.
Composability. Everything is designed to interlock. Types flow from one layer to the next, stores abstract boiler plate, and hooks bind elements auto-magically.

items.label: Complete theme system
items.text: Design language coded into a single React provider, with a fully customizable token system across colors, spacing, motion, icons, type ...

items.label: 40+ components
items.text: inputs, layout, media, overlays, and upload handling with a shared theme token system (colors, spacing, motion, type)

items.label: Real-time communication layer
items.text: production-grade abstractions over WebRTC, WebSocket, and SSE. ICE negotiation, reconnection logic, and typed event handlers handled for you

items.label: Browser API hooks
items.text: microphone, camera, screen share, IndexedDB, and audio visualisation, audio recording, each exposing clean React interfaces with automatic cleanup

items.label: SSR compatible
items.text: full React 18/19 RSC support, with 'use client' directives preserved through the build so Next.js and Remix apps work without configuration

items.label: Performance optimized
items.text: Abstracted web workers for threading uploads and components designed with fast mount / re-mount times of no more than 2 ms.

sections.title: A hard problem - the build system

blocks.text: The package ships 98 granular export paths so consumers only pay for what they use. Getting that to work — dual CJS/ESM output, matching TypeScript definitions, and correct chunk splitting — required writing custom Rollup config that generates every entry point dynamically.
Tradeoff: longer build times but dramatically smaller footprint on the consuming side. Worth it.

Abstracting WebRTC properly meant understanding it deeply first — ICE negotiation, track replacement without renegotiation, data channel lifecycle. The API surface had to hide that complexity without hiding control. Getting that balance right took several iterations.

I also underestimated how much of the work in a public package is the documentation and DX, not the code. The Storybook site, documentation, the contributor guides, the export map — that's more than half the work.
Sole author and maintainer — component API design, build engineering, documentation, CI/CD, and the npm publishing lifecycle across 34 releases.
